nameStory: The name 'white morning-glory' perfectly describes this vine's small, pure white trumpet-shaped flowers that open in the early morning hours, just like their more colorful cousins. The scientific name 'lacunosa' comes from a Latin word meaning 'air spaces,' referring to the distinctive pattern of veins in the leaves that create little pockets or gaps.
description: White morning-glory is a small annual vine that twists and climbs its way through gardens, fields, and disturbed areas. Unlike the showy purple or blue morning-glories you might know, this one produces dainty white flowers that are noticeably smaller than most of its relatives. The vine has heart-shaped leaves and a delicate, wiry appearance as it spirals around fence posts, other plants, or anything it can grab onto with its twining stems.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white trumpet-shaped flowers, much tinier than typical morning-glories, with five fused petals forming a funnel that's about the size of a nickel

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped leaves with pointed tips and distinctive veining that creates visible air pockets or gaps between the leaf veins when held up to light

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Slender twining vine that spirals counterclockwise around supports, feeling smooth and flexible to the touch with a wiry, delicate texture

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small round seed capsules that split open when ripe, revealing dark seeds inside the papery brown pod

habitat: White morning-glory thrives in disturbed soils like garden edges, roadsides, and waste areas throughout New England, though it's quite rare in our region. It prefers full sun and well-drained soil, often appearing in cultivated areas, along fence rows, and in fields where the soil has been disturbed.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring when soil warms up, with young vines beginning their characteristic spiraling growth pattern.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering occurs in mid to late summer, with small white flowers opening in early morning and often closing by afternoon on hot days.
seasonality.fall: Seed capsules mature and split open in early fall, releasing seeds before the first frost kills the annual vine.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back completely, leaving only seeds in the soil to sprout the following spring.

funFact: This morning-glory is actually closely related to the sweet potato - they're both in the same genus! While one cousin grows underground tubers we love to eat, this one puts all its energy into producing those delicate white flowers and climbing toward the sun.
confusionNotes: The small white flowers immediately separate this from the common purple, blue, or pink morning-glories most people know. The key difference is size - if your morning-glory flowers are tiny and white rather than large and colorful, you've likely found this species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being native to the United States, white morning-glory is extremely rare in New England, with only one recorded observation in our region. Most morning-glories people encounter here are actually the more common non-native species with larger, colorful flowers.
compareHints: White morning-glory stands out from its Ipomoea relatives by having the smallest flowers in the genus - much tinier than the dinner-plate-sized blooms of moonflower or the vibrant purple trumpets of common morning-glory. While wild potato vine also has white flowers, those are much larger and the plant produces thick, fleshy underground roots unlike this delicate annual.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common morning-glory has the largest flowers among New England's morning-glories, with those distinctive heart-shaped leaves that lack the three-lobed structure of ivy-leaved morning-glory.

Among New England morning-glories, ivy-leaved is distinguished by its three-lobed leaves - common morning-glory has unlobed heart-shaped leaves, while white morning-glory has much smaller flowers and often heart-shaped but sometimes three-lobed leaves.

Garden Morning Glory stands out from its Ipomoea cousins with its large flower size and vibrant blue color range - Common Morning Glory has smaller, more purple-pink flowers, while Ivy-leaved Morning Glory has distinctly lobed leaves rather than the simple heart shape.
Cypress vine is instantly distinguished from all other morning glories by its incredibly fine, thread-like leaf segments - every other morning glory in New England has broad, solid leaves.

Among its morning glory relatives, moonflower stands out for its exclusively nighttime blooming and pure white color - most other Ipomoea species bloom during the day in shades of purple, blue, pink, or red.
Unlike its morning glory relatives that are primarily grown for their showy trumpet flowers, sweet potato is grown for foliage and edible tubers, rarely flowering in New England's climate.
Red morning glory stands out from other New England morning glories primarily by its small size and brilliant red color - most others have much larger purple, blue, or white flowers.
Among New England morning-glories, wild potato vine stands out with its pure white flowers that have pink throats, while most others have purple, blue, or pink flowers.

Among New England morning glories, scarlet creeper is the only one with consistently bright red flowers - common morning glory has purple flowers, ivy-leaved morning glory has blue to purple blooms, and moonflower has large white flowers.
